meta.doctrine: Authority mathematical rule book imported from Math generator. Teach rules (form + operation + examples). Apply by decomposition — not Q/A stuffing.

rules.name: Numeral denotes value
preconditions: n is a valid numeral in the active numeral system
rules.operation: Interpret the numeral as the value represented by its digits and sign.
examples: 4 denotes four
-12 denotes negative twelve
3.5 denotes three and one half
counterexamples: 3..4 is not a valid numeral
--7 is not a numeral in strict mode
common_errors: Treating notation artifacts as values

rules.name: Place value in base 10
rules.output_form: sum of digits times powers of ten
preconditions: Each d_i is a digit from 0 to 9
rules.operation: Interpret the numeral as the sum of each digit multiplied by its place value.
counterexamples: Digit 12 inside a single decimal place is invalid

rules.name: Equality reflexive
preconditions: Equality relation is defined in the domain
rules.operation: Every object equals itself.

rules.name: Equality symmetric
preconditions: a = b is true
rules.operation: Reverse a true equality without changing truth value.

rules.name: Equality transitive
preconditions: a = b is true
b = c is true
rules.operation: Compose equalities transitively.

rules.name: Order comparison on ordered domains
preconditions: The domain has an order relation
rules.operation: Evaluate the order relation between two values.
counterexamples: i < 1 is invalid in C under standard ordering
common_errors: Assuming all numeric domains are ordered

rules.name: Unary plus
rules.operation: Unary plus leaves value unchanged.

rules.name: Unary minus
preconditions: The domain supports additive inverses
rules.operation: Produce the additive inverse of the operand.
examples: -5 is the inverse of 5
counterexamples: Unary minus on a natural number may leave the natural-number domain

rules.name: Double negative
rules.operation: Two additive inversions cancel.

rules.name: Addition closure by domain
preconditions: a and b belong to a domain closed under addition
rules.operation: Add two values within a domain closed under addition.
examples: 2 + 3 in N is valid
-4 + 9 in Z is valid
1/2 + 1/3 in Q is valid
counterexamples: Adding incompatible object types is invalid
common_errors: Ignoring domain mismatch

rules.name: Addition commutative
rules.operation: Swap operands in addition without changing value.
counterexamples: String concatenation is not arithmetic addition

rules.name: Addition associative
rules.operation: Regroup addition without changing value.

rules.name: Additive identity
rules.operation: Adding zero leaves the value unchanged.

rules.name: Additive inverse
preconditions: The additive inverse exists in the domain
rules.operation: Add a number to its additive inverse.
counterexamples: In N without negatives, -6 is outside the domain

rules.name: Atomic addition of small naturals
preconditions: Operands are small natural-number counts
rules.operation: Combine counts directly.
counterexamples: 2 + 2 = 5 is false

rules.name: Column addition with carry
preconditions: Operands are written in positional notation
rules.operation: Add digits by place from right to left and carry when the partial sum reaches the base.
counterexamples: Failing to add the carry gives 95, which is false
common_errors: Dropping the carry digit

rules.name: Fraction addition with common denominator
rules.operation: Add numerators while keeping the common denominator.
common_errors: Multiplying denominators unnecessarily

rules.name: Fraction addition with different denominators
rules.operation: Convert to a common denominator and add the adjusted numerators.
common_errors: Adding numerator to numerator and denominator to denominator

rules.name: Decimal addition
preconditions: Decimal places are aligned
rules.operation: Align decimal places and then add positionally.
common_errors: Misaligning decimal points

rules.name: Subtraction as additive inverse
rules.operation: Rewrite subtraction as addition of the additive inverse.

rules.name: Subtraction identity
rules.operation: Subtracting zero leaves the value unchanged.

rules.name: Self-subtraction
rules.operation: Subtract a value from itself.

rules.name: Subtraction is not commutative
rules.operation: Record that swapping subtraction operands changes the result in general.
counterexamples: Equal operands are a special case: 4 - 4 = 4 - 4
common_errors: Swapping operands as if subtraction behaved like addition

rules.name: Borrowing in positional subtraction
preconditions: Operands are written in positional notation
rules.operation: Borrow from the next higher place when the current digit is too small.
counterexamples: 52 - 38 = 26 is false
common_errors: Forgetting to decrement the higher place after borrowing

rules.name: Natural-number subtraction restriction
preconditions: a and b are natural numbers
rules.operation: If a < b, subtraction may fail in N and require promotion to Z.
examples: 3 - 5 is not in N
common_errors: Assuming subtraction always stays inside N

rules.name: Multiplication closure
preconditions: The domain is closed under multiplication
rules.operation: Multiply two values in a multiplicatively closed domain.
examples: 3 * 4 in N is valid
(-2) * 5 in Z is valid

rules.name: Multiplication commutative
rules.operation: Swap multiplication operands without changing value.

rules.name: Multiplication associative
rules.operation: Regroup multiplication without changing value.

rules.name: Multiplicative identity
rules.operation: Multiplying by one leaves value unchanged.

rules.name: Zero product with zero operand
rules.operation: Any value multiplied by zero gives zero.
counterexamples: 937 * 0 = 937 is false

rules.name: Repeated addition interpretation
rules.output_form: a added to itself b times
preconditions: b is a whole-number count
rules.operation: Interpret multiplication as repeated addition in whole-number contexts.
counterexamples: This interpretation does not directly define 4 * 1/2
common_errors: Overextending repeated addition to all domains without redefinition

rules.name: Sign rules for multiplication
rules.operation: Determine the sign of a product from operand signs.
common_errors: Treating negative times negative as negative

rules.name: Distributive law
rules.operation: Distribute multiplication over addition.
common_errors: Failing to distribute to every term

rules.name: Fraction multiplication
rules.operation: Multiply numerators and denominators.

rules.name: Decimal multiplication
rules.operation: Multiply as integers, then place the decimal according to total decimal places.
common_errors: Misplacing the decimal point

rules.name: Division as inverse multiplication
rules.operation: Rewrite division as multiplication by a reciprocal when the reciprocal is defined.

rules.name: Division by one
rules.operation: Dividing by one leaves the value unchanged.

rules.name: Zero dividend
rules.operation: Zero divided by a nonzero divisor is zero.
common_errors: Confusing 0/a with a/0

rules.name: Division by zero forbidden
rules.operation: Reject division by zero as undefined in standard arithmetic.
examples: 5 / 0 is invalid
0 / 0 is invalid and indeterminate in many extended contexts
counterexamples: 5 / 0 = 0 is false
5 / 0 = infinity is not standard arithmetic equality
common_errors: Assigning an ordinary numeric value to division by zero

rules.name: Division is not commutative
rules.operation: Record that swapping dividend and divisor changes the value in general.

rules.name: Division is not associative
rules.operation: Record that regrouping division changes value in general.

rules.name: Exact division in integers
preconditions: b divides a
rules.operation: When the divisor divides the dividend evenly, the quotient remains in Z.
counterexamples: 7 / 2 is not an integer, though it is valid in Q and equals 7/2

rules.name: Fraction well-formedness
rules.operation: Recognize a rational fraction only when the denominator is nonzero.
examples: 3/4 is valid
counterexamples: 3/0 is invalid

rules.name: Equivalent fractions
rules.operation: Multiply numerator and denominator by the same nonzero factor.
counterexamples: 2/3 = 4/7 is false

rules.name: Fraction reduction
preconditions: numerator and denominator share a nonzero common factor
rules.operation: Divide numerator and denominator by a common factor.
common_errors: Cancelling terms that are not common factors

rules.name: Improper fraction to mixed number
preconditions: a > b
a = qb + r
rules.operation: Rewrite an improper positive fraction as a whole-number part plus a proper fraction.
counterexamples: 11/4 = 3 3/4 is false

rules.name: Fraction comparison by common denominator
rules.operation: Compare fractions by converting to a common denominator or cross-multiplying when valid.

rules.name: Decimal to fraction conversion
preconditions: The decimal expansion is finite
rules.operation: Convert a finite decimal to a rational fraction and reduce if desired.

rules.name: Fraction to decimal conversion
preconditions: Denominator is nonzero
rules.operation: Divide numerator by denominator to obtain a terminating or repeating decimal.

rules.name: Trailing zero invariance
rules.operation: Appending trailing zeros after the decimal point does not change value.
common_errors: Confusing place value when inserting zeros inside the decimal

rules.name: Ratio interpretation
preconditions: b != 0 for ratio-to-fraction conversion
rules.operation: Interpret a ratio as a comparison and, when appropriate, as a fraction.
examples: 2:3 corresponds to 2/3

rules.name: Percentage definition
rules.operation: Interpret percent as per hundred.
counterexamples: 25% = 25 is false

rules.name: Percentage of quantity
rules.operation: Compute a percentage of a quantity by converting the percent to a fraction or decimal multiplier.
counterexamples: 15% of 80 = 120 is false

rules.name: Positive integer exponent
preconditions: n is a positive integer
rules.operation: Interpret positive integer exponentiation as repeated multiplication.

rules.name: Exponent identity one
rules.operation: Exponent one returns the base.

rules.name: Exponent zero
rules.operation: A nonzero base raised to the zero power equals one.
counterexamples: 0^0 must not be silently forced to 1 in this rule set
common_errors: Applying the zero-exponent rule to 0^0 without context

rules.name: Product of same base
preconditions: Expressions share the same base
Exponents are in a domain where the rule is valid
rules.operation: Add exponents when multiplying like bases.
common_errors: Using the rule on unlike bases

rules.name: Power of power
rules.operation: Multiply exponents when raising a power to another power.

rules.name: Product power rule
rules.operation: Distribute an exponent over a product when the rule is valid in the domain.

rules.name: Negative exponent
rules.operation: Rewrite a negative exponent as the reciprocal of a positive exponent.
counterexamples: 0^(-1) is invalid

rules.name: Square root over reals
rules.operation: Return the principal square root in the real numbers.
examples: sqrt(9) = 3
sqrt(0) = 0
counterexamples: sqrt(9) = -3 is false under principal-root convention
sqrt(-1) is invalid in real-only mode
common_errors: Confusing the equation y^2 = x with the principal root function

rules.name: nth root domain rule
rules.output_form: root value if domain allows it
preconditions: Validity depends on parity of n and active domain
rules.operation: Determine root existence and value from degree parity and domain.
examples: cube_root(-8) = -2 in R
fourth_root(16) = 2 as principal root in R
counterexamples: fourth_root(-16) is invalid in R

rules.name: Root and power interaction
rules.operation: Simplify the square root of a square in the reals using absolute value.
counterexamples: sqrt(a^2) = a is false in general over R
common_errors: Dropping the absolute value

rules.name: Absolute value definition
rules.operation: Return a if a is nonnegative and -a if a is negative.

rules.name: Nonnegativity of absolute value
rules.operation: Absolute value is never negative in ordered real-like domains.

rules.name: Product rule for absolute value
rules.operation: Distribute absolute value over multiplication.

rules.name: Explicit grouping first
rules.operation: Evaluate grouped subexpressions before surrounding operations.
counterexamples: 2*(3+4) = 10 is false

rules.name: Exponent before multiplication and addition
rules.operation: Apply exponentiation before multiplication and addition unless grouping overrides it.
counterexamples: ((2+3)^2)*4 is a different expression

rules.name: Multiplication and division before addition and subtraction
rules.operation: Apply multiplication and division before addition and subtraction unless grouping overrides it.
counterexamples: (2+3)*4 = 20 is not equal to 2 + 3*4

rules.name: Left-to-right for equal precedence
rules.operation: Evaluate multiplication/division and addition/subtraction left to right when precedence is equal.
counterexamples: 8 / (4 * 2) = 1 is a different grouped expression

rules.name: Minimal domain promotion
preconditions: Automatic promotion is enabled
rules.operation: Promote to the smallest standard domain that contains the result.
examples: 3 - 5 promotes from N to Z
1 / 2 promotes from Z to Q
sqrt(2) promotes from Q to R
sqrt(-1) promotes from R to C

rules.name: Domain failure without promotion
preconditions: Automatic promotion is disabled
rules.operation: Emit a domain error instead of silently changing domains.
examples: In strict natural-number mode, 3 - 5 is a domain error

rules.name: Invalid fraction addition heuristic
rules.operation: Mark this pattern as invalid.
common_errors: Adding numerator to numerator and denominator to denominator

rules.name: Cancelling across addition is invalid
rules.operation: Mark cancellation across addition as invalid.
common_errors: Cancelling terms that are not multiplicative factors

rules.name: Square root distribution error
rules.operation: Mark naive square-root distribution over addition as invalid.
counterexamples: sqrt(9+16) = 5, but sqrt(9) + sqrt(16) = 7

rules.name: Division by zero shortcut error
rules.operation: Mark assigning zero to division by zero as invalid.
counterexamples: 5/0 is undefined, not 0

rules.name: Divisibility definition
rules.output_form: exists integer k with a = bk
rules.operation: Interpret divisibility by existence of an integer multiplier.
examples: 3 divides 12 because 12 = 3*4
counterexamples: 2 does not divide 7 in Z

rules.name: Prime number criterion
preconditions: p > 1 for primality
rules.operation: Classify p as prime when its only positive divisors are 1 and p.
examples: 2, 3, and 5 are prime
counterexamples: 1 is not prime
9 is not prime because 3 divides 9

rules.name: Greatest common divisor
preconditions: a and b are not both zero
rules.operation: Return the greatest positive integer dividing both a and b.
counterexamples: gcd(12,18) = 3 is not greatest

rules.name: Least common multiple
rules.operation: Return the least positive integer divisible by both a and b.
counterexamples: 48 is a common multiple of 6 and 8, but not the least one

rules.name: Modular congruence
rules.input_form: a congruent to b mod n
rules.operation: Interpret congruence modulo n as divisibility of the difference by n.
examples: 17 is congruent to 5 modulo 12
counterexamples: 17 is not congruent to 6 modulo 12

rules.name: Signed change in word problems
rules.input_form: gains and losses as signed quantities
preconditions: Positive and negative directions are declared consistently
rules.operation: Represent gains as positive and losses as negative, then add signed quantities.
examples: A gain of 8 and a loss of 3 produce net change 5
counterexamples: Treating every change as positive loses direction information

rules.name: Unit-aware addition
rules.output_form: sum in a common compatible unit
preconditions: Units are identical or converted to a compatible common unit first
rules.operation: Add measured quantities only after unit compatibility has been established.
examples: 2 meters + 30 centimeters = 2.3 meters
counterexamples: 2 meters + 3 seconds is invalid as ordinary addition of physical quantities

rules.name: Variable as domain-bound placeholder
rules.output_form: symbolic placeholder over an allowed domain
preconditions: The variable has an active or inferable domain
rules.operation: Interpret the variable as an unspecified value ranging over its domain.
examples: x in x + 1 is a variable
x in x belongs to R is real-valued if declared over R
counterexamples: Treating x as a fixed numeric literal without assignment is invalid
common_errors: Using a variable with no domain in a domain-sensitive rule

rules.name: Constant symbol in expression
preconditions: The constant symbol has an agreed meaning in context
rules.operation: Keep the named constant fixed across the expression context.
examples: pi is constant across pi*r^2
e is constant in e^x
counterexamples: Treating pi as a variable to solve unless explicitly redefined is invalid

rules.name: Expression formation
preconditions: Operators and operands are arranged under syntax rules
rules.operation: Form an algebraic expression from valid symbolic pieces.
counterexamples: +*x is not a valid algebraic expression

rules.name: Term structure
rules.input_form: coefficient times variable part or constant
rules.operation: Recognize a term as either a standalone constant or a coefficient multiplied by a variable part.
examples: 3x is a term
-7 is a constant term
2xy is a term
counterexamples: x + y is not a single term

rules.name: Coefficient identification
preconditions: The target is a term with a variable part or an implied coefficient
rules.operation: Identify the scalar multiplier attached to the variable part.
examples: Coefficient of 7x is 7
Coefficient of -x is -1
counterexamples: In x + 2, the coefficient of x is not 2

rules.name: Monomial well-formedness
rules.input_form: single term with coefficient and nonnegative integer powers
preconditions: Exponents are nonnegative integers in the basic polynomial setting
rules.operation: Recognize a monomial in the ordinary polynomial setting.
examples: 4x^2y is a monomial
-3 is a monomial
counterexamples: 1/x is not a monomial in the ordinary polynomial ring over x

rules.name: Polynomial well-formedness
preconditions: The sum is finite and each term is a monomial
rules.operation: Recognize a polynomial in the ordinary polynomial setting.
examples: x^2 + 3x + 2 is a polynomial
5 is a polynomial
counterexamples: x^-1 + 2 is not a polynomial in the ordinary polynomial setting

rules.name: Direct substitution
rules.input_form: expression with variable x and assignment for x
rules.output_form: expression with every x replaced consistently
preconditions: The substitution target is well-formed
The substituted value respects the variable domain
rules.operation: Replace a variable by a value or expression consistently across the target expression.
examples: If x = 3, then 2x + 1 becomes 7
If x = y + 1, then x^2 becomes (y + 1)^2
counterexamples: Replacing x in only some occurrences of x is invalid
common_errors: Failing to preserve grouping after substitution

rules.name: Substitution requires parentheses for compound expressions
preconditions: The substituted value is a compound expression
rules.operation: Wrap substituted compound expressions in grouping when needed to preserve structure.
examples: Substitute x = a + b into 3x to obtain 3(a + b)
counterexamples: 3x with x = a + b becoming 3a + b is invalid

rules.name: Like-term criterion
rules.operation: Treat two terms as like terms only when they have identical variable parts with identical exponents.
examples: 3x and -2x are like terms
5x^2y and 9x^2y are like terms
counterexamples: 3x and 3x^2 are not like terms
2xy and 2x are not like terms

rules.name: Combine like terms
rules.input_form: sum or difference of like terms
preconditions: Terms are like terms
rules.operation: Add or subtract coefficients while preserving the common variable part.
counterexamples: 3x + 2y = 5xy is invalid
common_errors: Combining unlike terms by multiplying variables together

rules.name: Constant combination
rules.input_form: expression with constants and variable terms
rules.operation: Combine constant terms using arithmetic rules independently of variable terms.
counterexamples: x + 2 + 5 = 8x is invalid

rules.name: Distributive expansion
preconditions: Multiplication distributes over addition in the active structure
rules.operation: Expand multiplication across a sum.
examples: x(y + z) = xy + xz
counterexamples: 3(x + 2) = 3x + 2 is invalid
common_errors: Failing to distribute to every term

rules.name: Reverse distribution by common factor
preconditions: A common factor exists in all terms
rules.operation: Factor out a common multiplicative factor.
examples: xy + xz = x(y + z)
counterexamples: 6x + 9 = 3(x + 3) is invalid

rules.name: Square of a sum
rules.operation: Expand the square of a binomial sum.
counterexamples: (a + b)^2 = a^2 + b^2 is invalid in general
common_errors: Dropping the middle term

rules.name: Difference of squares
rules.operation: Factor a difference of squares.
counterexamples: x^2 - 9 = (x - 9)^2 is invalid

rules.name: Equation equivalence by same addition
preconditions: Both sides and the added term are defined in compatible domains
rules.operation: Add the same quantity to both sides of an equation.
counterexamples: Adding different values to each side does not preserve equivalence

rules.name: Equation equivalence by same subtraction
preconditions: Both sides and the subtracted term are defined in compatible domains
rules.operation: Subtract the same quantity from both sides of an equation.

rules.name: Equation equivalence by same nonzero multiplication
preconditions: The multiplier is defined in the domain
rules.operation: Multiply both sides of an equation by the same quantity.
counterexamples: Multiplying by an undefined quantity is invalid

rules.name: Equation equivalence by same nonzero division
rules.operation: Divide both sides of an equation by the same nonzero quantity.
counterexamples: Dividing both sides by 0 is invalid

rules.name: Transposition as derived operation
rules.input_form: equation with term moved across equality
rules.output_form: equivalent equation with inverse operation applied
preconditions: The move is shorthand for a valid balance operation on both sides
rules.operation: Interpret transposition as adding the inverse or subtracting the same quantity on both sides.
examples: x + 5 = 9 becomes x = 9 - 5
x - 3 = 7 becomes x = 7 + 3
counterexamples: x + 5 = 9 becoming x = 9 + 5 is invalid
common_errors: Changing sides without changing sign correctly

rules.name: Solve ax + b = c
rules.operation: Isolate the variable term and divide by the nonzero coefficient.
counterexamples: 2x + 3 = 11 -> x = 11 - 3 = 8 is invalid
common_errors: Failing to divide after isolating the variable term

rules.name: Solve x/a = b
rules.operation: Multiply both sides by the denominator coefficient.
counterexamples: x/5 = 3 -> x = 3/5 is invalid

rules.name: Verify candidate solution
preconditions: The candidate is in the original domain or explicitly rejected for domain reasons
rules.operation: Substitute the candidate into the original equation and test truth.
examples: For 2x + 3 = 11, test x = 4: true
counterexamples: Accepting a derived value without checking domain restrictions can be invalid

rules.name: Zero-product property
preconditions: The active structure has no zero divisors in the intended sense
rules.operation: Infer factor-wise zero conditions from a zero product.
examples: (x - 2)(x + 3) = 0 implies x = 2 or x = -3
counterexamples: ab = 6 does not imply a = 6 or b = 6

rules.name: Zero-product solving pattern
preconditions: The left side is correctly factorized
The zero-product property applies
rules.operation: Factor the equation and set each factor equal to zero.
counterexamples: x^2 + x - 6 = 0 -> x + 3 = x - 2 = 0 is invalid notation and invalid reasoning

rules.name: Invalid distribution of exponent over addition
rules.operation: Mark naive exponent distribution over addition as invalid in general.

rules.name: Invalid cancellation across addition
rules.operation: Mark cancellation across addition as invalid in general.
counterexamples: (x + 2)/x is not 2 in general

rules.name: Invalid square root simplification
rules.operation: Mark dropping the absolute value from sqrt(x^2) as invalid over the reals.
counterexamples: If x = -3, sqrt(x^2) = 3, not -3

rules.name: System as simultaneous algebraic constraint
rules.output_form: conjunction of equations on one shared assignment
preconditions: All variables are interpreted in a shared active domain
rules.operation: Interpret a system as equations that must all hold simultaneously for the same assignment.
examples: x + y = 3 and x - y = 1 must both hold for the same ordered pair
counterexamples: Choosing one variable value from one equation and another incompatible value from the second is invalid

rules.name: Polynomial division identity
rules.output_form: f = gq + r with degree(r) < degree(g)
preconditions: g is a nonzero polynomial
rules.operation: Express polynomial division by quotient and remainder.
examples: x^2 - 1 divided by x - 1 gives quotient x + 1 and remainder 0
counterexamples: A remainder with degree not less than the divisor degree is invalid

rules.name: Remainder theorem
preconditions: The divisor has the form x-a
rules.operation: Identify the remainder of division by x-a as the polynomial value at a.
examples: For f(x) = x^2 - 1, division by x - 1 has remainder f(1) = 0
counterexamples: Using the theorem on a divisor not normalized to x-a is invalid without rewriting

rules.name: Rational expression domain exclusion
preconditions: Denominators are explicit or inferable
rules.operation: Exclude every value that makes a denominator zero before simplifying or solving.
examples: In (x + 1)/(x - 2), x = 2 is excluded
counterexamples: Cancelling a factor and forgetting the original exclusion is invalid

rules.name: Rational simplification preserves exclusions
rules.output_form: simplified form with original exclusions preserved
preconditions: A common factor was cancelled from numerator and denominator
rules.operation: Carry all original denominator exclusions into the simplified result.
examples: (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) simplifies to x + 2 with x != 2
counterexamples: Replacing the expression by x + 2 over all reals is invalid

rules.name: Completing the square
preconditions: The quadratic coefficient of x^2 is 1 or has been normalized first
rules.operation: Rewrite the quadratic by introducing and compensating for the square of half the linear coefficient.
counterexamples: x^2 + 6x + 5 = (x + 6)^2 - 31 is invalid

rules.name: Quadratic formula
rules.operation: Solve a quadratic equation using the quadratic formula.
examples: x^2 - 5x + 6 = 0 gives x = 2 or x = 3
counterexamples: Dividing only by a instead of 2a is invalid

rules.name: Function evaluation
preconditions: a belongs to the domain of f
rules.operation: Substitute the argument into the defining rule of the function and simplify.
examples: If f(x) = x^2 + 1, then f(3) = 10
counterexamples: Evaluating f(a) when a is outside the domain is invalid
common_errors: Ignoring domain restrictions

rules.name: Piecewise function branch selection
preconditions: Exactly one branch condition is satisfied at the point of evaluation
rules.operation: Evaluate a piecewise function by selecting the unique branch whose condition is satisfied.
examples: If f(x) = x^2 for x >= 0 and -x for x < 0, then f(-3) = 3
counterexamples: Applying multiple branches at once is invalid

rules.name: Piecewise boundary check
rules.operation: Check branch conditions at boundary points before evaluation, limit analysis, or continuity claims.
examples: For a branch split at x = 0, evaluate whether 0 belongs to the left or right rule exactly as stated
counterexamples: Assuming x < 0 includes x = 0 is invalid

rules.name: Limit of a constant
rules.operation: The limit of a constant equals the constant.

rules.name: Limit of the identity function
rules.operation: The limit of the identity function at a is a.

rules.name: Sum rule for limits
preconditions: Both component limits exist at the same point
rules.operation: Take the limit termwise across addition.
counterexamples: Using the rule when component limits do not exist is invalid

rules.name: Product rule for limits
preconditions: Both component limits exist at the same point
rules.operation: Take the limit termwise across multiplication.

rules.name: Quotient rule for limits
preconditions: Both component limits exist at the same point
The denominator limit is not zero
rules.operation: Take the limit termwise across division when the denominator limit is nonzero.
counterexamples: Using the quotient rule when the denominator limit is 0 is invalid

rules.name: Direct substitution for continuous expressions
preconditions: The expression is continuous at a
rules.operation: Compute the limit by direct substitution when continuity permits it.
counterexamples: Direct substitution into 0/0 does not resolve the limit

rules.name: One-sided limit agreement
rules.input_form: left and right limits at a point
rules.output_form: two-sided limit exists iff they are equal
preconditions: Both one-sided limits exist
rules.operation: Determine a two-sided limit from left-hand and right-hand limits.
examples: For |x| at 0, both one-sided limits are 0, so the two-sided limit is 0
counterexamples: If left and right limits differ, the two-sided limit does not exist

rules.name: Continuity at a point
rules.operation: Check that f(a) exists, the limit exists, and the limit equals the function value.
examples: f(x) = x^2 is continuous at every real number
counterexamples: A removable hole where f(a) is missing is not continuity at a

rules.name: Piecewise continuity check
preconditions: The point is a branch boundary
rules.operation: Compare left-hand limit, right-hand limit, and function value at the branch boundary.
examples: Piecewise definitions split at x = 0 require left-limit, right-limit, and function-value comparison at 0
counterexamples: Checking only one branch is insufficient

rules.name: Derivative by limit definition
preconditions: The limit exists
rules.operation: Define the derivative as the limit of the difference quotient.
examples: For f(x) = x^2, f'(x) = 2x from the limit definition
counterexamples: If the limit does not exist, the derivative does not exist at that point

rules.name: Derivative of a constant
rules.operation: Differentiate a constant with respect to the active variable.
examples: d/dx 7 = 0

rules.name: Power rule
preconditions: n is in a class where the rule is valid under the active interpretation
rules.operation: Differentiate a power of x using the power rule.
examples: d/dx x^5 = 5x^4
counterexamples: d/dx x^5 = x^4 is invalid

rules.name: Constant multiple rule
rules.operation: Pull out constant scalar multiples during differentiation.

rules.name: Sum rule for derivatives
preconditions: Both derivatives exist
rules.operation: Differentiate a sum termwise.

rules.name: Product rule
preconditions: Both derivatives exist
rules.operation: Differentiate a product using the product rule.
examples: d/dx [x sin(x)] = sin(x) + x cos(x)
counterexamples: d/dx [fg] = f'g' is invalid

rules.name: Quotient rule
preconditions: Both derivatives exist
rules.operation: Differentiate a quotient using the quotient rule.
counterexamples: d/dx [f/g] = f'/g' is invalid

rules.name: Chain rule
preconditions: The outer and inner derivatives exist
rules.operation: Differentiate a composition using the chain rule.
counterexamples: Differentiating only the outer or only the inner function is incomplete

rules.name: Partial derivative with respect to one variable
preconditions: Variables not named in the derivative are treated as independent constants
rules.operation: Differentiate with respect to one variable while holding the others fixed.
examples: partial/partial x (x^2 y + y^3) = 2xy
counterexamples: Differentiating y^3 with respect to x as 3y^2 is invalid when y is independent of x

rules.name: Indefinite integral as antiderivative family
preconditions: F'(x) = f(x)
rules.operation: Represent an indefinite integral as the family of antiderivatives.
examples: int 2x dx = x^2 + C
counterexamples: Omitting the integration constant in an indefinite integral loses the full family

rules.name: Power rule for indefinite integrals
rules.operation: Integrate a power using the standard antiderivative rule.
examples: int x^3 dx = x^4/4 + C
counterexamples: int x^-1 dx does not use this rule in the ordinary real setting

rules.name: Linearity of the integral
rules.output_form: a int f(x) dx + b int g(x) dx
rules.operation: Distribute the integral over sums and pull out constants.
examples: int (2x + 3) dx = x^2 + 3x + C

rules.name: Definite integral over zero width interval
rules.operation: A definite integral over an interval of zero length is zero.
examples: int_2^2 x^2 dx = 0

rules.name: Reversal of bounds
rules.operation: Reverse integration bounds at the cost of a sign change.
examples: int_1^3 x dx = - int_3^1 x dx

rules.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part I
preconditions: F'(x) = f(x)
The theorem's regularity assumptions hold
rules.operation: Evaluate a definite integral by an antiderivative.
examples: int_0^1 2x dx = 1
counterexamples: Applying antiderivative evaluation without checking differentiability assumptions can be invalid in edge cases

rules.name: Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part II
preconditions: Standard continuity assumptions hold
rules.operation: Differentiate an integral with variable upper bound.
examples: d/dx int_0^x t^2 dt = x^2

rules.name: Finite summation expansion
preconditions: m and n are concrete integer bounds with m <= n
rules.operation: Expand a finite indexed summation into its explicit term list.
counterexamples: Expanding without respecting the index range is invalid

rules.name: Linearity of finite summation
preconditions: The sums are finite and share the same bounds
rules.operation: Distribute finite summation over addition.

rules.name: Finite product expansion
preconditions: m and n are concrete integer bounds with m <= n
rules.operation: Expand a finite indexed product into its explicit factor list.

rules.name: Geometric series closed form
rules.operation: Apply the finite geometric series formula.
counterexamples: Applying the formula with r = 1 is invalid

rules.name: Infinite geometric series convergence rule
rules.operation: Apply the standard convergence formula for an infinite geometric series.
examples: sum_{k=0}^{infinity} (1/2)^k = 2
counterexamples: sum_{k=0}^{infinity} 2^k does not converge in the real numbers

rules.name: Derivative of sine
rules.operation: Differentiate sine with respect to its argument.
examples: d/dx sin(x) = cos(x)
counterexamples: d/dx sin(x) = -sin(x) is invalid

rules.name: Derivative of cosine
rules.operation: Differentiate cosine with respect to its argument.
examples: d/dx cos(x) = -sin(x)
counterexamples: d/dx cos(x) = sin(x) is invalid

rules.name: Basic trigonometric antiderivatives
rules.input_form: int sin(x) dx or int cos(x) dx
rules.operation: Apply the standard antiderivatives for sine and cosine.
examples: int cos(x) dx = sin(x) + C
counterexamples: int sin(x) dx = cos(x) + C is invalid

rules.name: L'Hopital-type limit rule
preconditions: The original limit is of type 0/0 or infinity/infinity
Differentiability and nonzero-denominator derivative conditions hold
rules.operation: Replace a qualifying indeterminate quotient limit by the limit of the quotient of derivatives.
examples: lim_{x->0} sin(x)/x = lim_{x->0} cos(x)/1 = 1
counterexamples: Applying the rule when the limit is not in an admissible indeterminate form is invalid

rules.name: Multivariable chain rule
rules.input_form: z = f(x,y), x = x(t), y = y(t)
preconditions: The needed partial derivatives and ordinary derivatives exist
rules.operation: Differentiate through every dependency path in a composed multivariable function.
examples: For z = x^2 + y^2 with x = t and y = t^2, dz/dt = 2x + 4ty after substitution
counterexamples: Differentiating through only one dependency path is invalid

rules.name: Invalid derivative of a product
rules.operation: Mark naive derivative splitting over products as invalid.

rules.name: Invalid derivative of a quotient
rules.operation: Mark naive derivative splitting over quotients as invalid.
counterexamples: d/dx [x/(x+1)] is not 1/1

rules.name: Invalid integral of a product by splitting
rules.output_form: int f(x) dx * int g(x) dx
rules.operation: Mark naive integral splitting over products as invalid.
counterexamples: int x*x dx is not (x^2/2)(x^2/2)

rules.name: Jacobian matrix formation
preconditions: The needed first partial derivatives exist
rules.operation: Assemble the Jacobian matrix from first partial derivatives of each component with respect to each variable.
counterexamples: Placing function values instead of partial derivatives into the Jacobian is invalid

rules.name: Ratio test for series
preconditions: The limit of |a_(n+1)/a_n| exists or is computable in the needed form
rules.operation: Use the ratio limit to certify absolute convergence for limits below 1 and divergence for limits above 1.
examples: For a_n = 1/n!, the ratio limit is 0, so the series converges absolutely
counterexamples: The case L = 1 is inconclusive by the ratio test alone

rules.name: Power-series termwise differentiation
preconditions: x lies inside the interval or disk of convergence
rules.operation: Differentiate a power series term by term within its convergence region.
examples: d/dx sum_{n=0}^{infinity} x^n = sum_{n=1}^{infinity} n x^(n-1) for |x| < 1
counterexamples: Applying termwise differentiation outside the convergence region is invalid

rules.name: Two distinct points determine a unique line
preconditions: A != B
rules.operation: Through two distinct points there exists exactly one line.
examples: Points A and B with A != B determine line AB
counterexamples: If A = B, no unique line is determined by the distinct-point rule

rules.name: Segment as bounded part of a line
rules.input_form: points A, B on a line
preconditions: A and B lie on a common line
rules.operation: Define the segment as the bounded part of the line between endpoints A and B inclusive.
examples: If A and B lie on a line, segment AB has finite length
counterexamples: Treating a segment as infinite in both directions is invalid

rules.name: Ray as directed half-line
preconditions: A != B
rules.operation: Define ray AB as starting at A and extending through B indefinitely.
examples: Ray AB and ray BA are different in standard orientation-sensitive notation
counterexamples: Treating ray AB as identical to segment AB is invalid

rules.name: Distance symmetry
rules.operation: Swap endpoints without changing unsigned distance.
examples: AB = BA as lengths
counterexamples: Directed vectors are not the same object as unsigned distance

rules.name: Segment length nonnegativity
rules.operation: Segment lengths are nonnegative and vanish only when endpoints coincide.
examples: If A != B then AB > 0
counterexamples: Assigning a negative segment length is invalid

rules.name: Angle measure additivity
rules.input_form: angle ABC split by interior point D
preconditions: D lies in the interior of angle ABC
rules.operation: Add adjacent interior angle measures to recover the whole angle.
examples: Splitting a 70 degree angle into 20 and 50 degrees preserves total measure
counterexamples: Adding nonadjacent angles without the interior-point condition is invalid

rules.name: Triangle angle sum
preconditions: The geometry is Euclidean
rules.operation: Apply the Euclidean triangle angle-sum rule.
examples: If angles are 50 and 60, the third angle is 70
counterexamples: Applying the Euclidean angle-sum rule unchanged in non-Euclidean settings is invalid

rules.name: Exterior angle theorem
rules.output_form: exterior angle equals sum of remote interior angles
rules.operation: Use the exterior-angle relation in a Euclidean triangle.
examples: If remote interior angles are 40 and 55, the exterior angle is 95
counterexamples: Using the adjacent interior angle instead of the remote pair is invalid

rules.name: Triangle inequality
rules.output_form: each side less than the sum of the other two
preconditions: a, b, c are interpreted as side lengths
rules.operation: Check whether three lengths can form a triangle.
examples: 3, 4, 5 satisfy triangle inequality
counterexamples: 1, 2, 4 do not form a triangle

rules.name: SSS congruence
rules.input_form: two triangles with three matching corresponding sides
preconditions: The side correspondence is valid
rules.operation: Infer triangle congruence from equality of all corresponding side lengths.
examples: Matching side triples 3,4,5 and 3,4,5 imply congruence under correspondence
counterexamples: Unmatched correspondence invalidates the claim

rules.name: SAS congruence
rules.input_form: two triangles with two sides and included angle matching
preconditions: The angle is included between the matched sides
rules.operation: Infer congruence from side-angle-side data.
examples: Equal side-angle-side data yields congruence
counterexamples: Using a nonincluded angle does not invoke SAS

rules.name: AA similarity
rules.input_form: two triangles with two equal corresponding angles
preconditions: The angle correspondence is valid
rules.operation: Infer triangle similarity from angle-angle data.
examples: Matching angles 40 and 60 imply similarity
counterexamples: Matching only one angle is insufficient

rules.name: Similar triangle side proportions
preconditions: The triangles are already known to be similar
rules.operation: Transfer similarity into proportional side-length relations.
examples: If scale factor is 2, corresponding side lengths double
counterexamples: Corresponding sides need not be equal unless the scale factor is 1

rules.name: Distance formula
preconditions: Coordinates are real-valued
rules.operation: Compute Euclidean distance in the Cartesian plane.
examples: Distance between (0,0) and (3,4) is 5
counterexamples: Adding raw coordinate differences without squaring is invalid

rules.name: Midpoint formula
preconditions: Coordinates are real-valued
rules.operation: Compute the midpoint of a segment in the Cartesian plane.
examples: Midpoint of (0,0) and (4,2) is (2,1)
counterexamples: Dividing only one coordinate sum by 2 is invalid

rules.name: Slope formula
rules.operation: Compute slope between two points with distinct x-coordinates.
examples: Slope through (1,2) and (3,6) is 2
counterexamples: Vertical lines do not have finite slope in the ordinary real-number sense

rules.name: Invalid triangle equality heuristic
rules.input_form: two matching sides in two triangles
rules.operation: Mark the inference from two side matches alone to full congruence as invalid in general.
counterexamples: Two sides alone do not determine a unique triangle in general

rules.name: Invalid coordinate distance shortcut
rules.operation: Mark Manhattan-distance substitution for Euclidean distance as invalid in this geometry setting.
counterexamples: Between (0,0) and (3,4), Euclidean distance is 5, not 7

rules.name: Radius-tangent perpendicularity
rules.input_form: circle center O, tangent point P
rules.output_form: OP perpendicular to tangent line at P
preconditions: The line is tangent to the circle at P
rules.operation: Use the radius-to-tangent perpendicularity fact at the point of tangency.
examples: If line l is tangent to circle O at P, then OP is perpendicular to l
counterexamples: A secant line through P is not justified as tangent by this rule alone

rules.name: Inscribed angle theorem
preconditions: The angle is inscribed in a circle
rules.operation: Relate an inscribed angle to its intercepted arc.
examples: An inscribed angle intercepting an 80 degree arc measures 40 degrees
counterexamples: Assigning the whole arc measure to the inscribed angle is invalid

rules.name: Triangle area formula
preconditions: Base and corresponding height are measured in compatible length units
rules.operation: Compute triangle area as one half times base times height.
examples: Triangle with base 10 and height 4 has area 20
counterexamples: Omitting the factor one half is invalid

rules.name: Circle area formula
rules.operation: Compute circle area from radius.
examples: Radius 3 gives area 9pi
counterexamples: 2pi r is circumference, not area

rules.name: Cylinder volume formula
rules.input_form: cylinder radius r and height h
rules.operation: Compute right circular cylinder volume from base radius and height.
examples: Radius 2 and height 5 give volume 20pi
counterexamples: Using pi r h omits one factor of r and is invalid

rules.name: Rigid motion preserves distance and angle measure
rules.input_form: translation, rotation, or reflection of a figure
preconditions: The transformation is a rigid motion
rules.operation: Use rigid-motion invariance to preserve lengths and angle measures.
examples: A translated triangle is congruent to the original triangle
counterexamples: A dilation with scale factor 2 does not preserve lengths

rules.name: Coordinate proof by slope or distance invariants
preconditions: The required coordinates and nondegeneracy conditions are defined
rules.operation: Use slope equality, negative reciprocal slopes, or equal distances as coordinate proof tools.
examples: Equal slopes show two nonvertical lines are parallel
counterexamples: Claiming perpendicularity from unequal slopes alone is invalid

rules.name: Circle standard form in coordinates
rules.output_form: circle with center (h,k) and radius r
rules.operation: Interpret the standard coordinate form of a circle.
examples: (x-1)^2 + (y+2)^2 = 9 has center (1,-2) and radius 3
counterexamples: A negative value of r^2 does not represent a real circle

rules.name: Parabola standard form
rules.operation: Interpret the vertical standard form of a parabola.
examples: y = 2(x-1)^2 + 3 has vertex (1,3)
counterexamples: Interpreting y = a(x-h)^2 + k as a circle is invalid

rules.name: System solution means simultaneous satisfaction
rules.output_form: assignment is a solution iff every equation is true simultaneously
preconditions: The assignment is defined for every system variable
rules.operation: Interpret a system solution as a simultaneous truth assignment for all equations.
examples: If a pair satisfies one equation but not the other, it is not a system solution
counterexamples: Solving equations independently and keeping incompatible assignments is invalid

rules.name: Linear equation form
preconditions: Variables do not multiply each other and appear only to first power
rules.operation: Recognize an equation as linear in its variables.
examples: 2x + 3y = 7 is linear
counterexamples: xy = 1 is not linear
x^2 + y = 4 is not linear

rules.name: Replace an equation by an equivalent equation
rules.input_form: system with one equation replaced by an equivalent equation
preconditions: The replacement equation is logically equivalent to the original equation in the active domain
rules.operation: Preserve the solution set by replacing an equation with an equivalent one.
examples: Replacing 2x = 8 with x = 4 preserves solutions
counterexamples: Replacing an equation with a nonequivalent statement changes the solution set

rules.name: Row-style combination rule
rules.input_form: system where one equation is replaced by itself plus a multiple of another
preconditions: The multiplier is defined in the active domain
rules.operation: Add a multiple of one equation to another without changing the solution set.
examples: From x + y = 3 and x - y = 1, subtracting the second from the first yields 2y = 2
counterexamples: Applying different uncontrolled transformations to both equations can break equivalence

rules.name: Isolate a variable in a simple equation
rules.input_form: linear equation with one easily isolated variable
rules.output_form: equivalent explicit expression for that variable
preconditions: The target variable has a nonzero coefficient and isolation is straightforward
rules.operation: Solve one equation for one variable in preparation for substitution.
examples: x + y = 3 becomes x = 3 - y
counterexamples: Isolating incorrectly, such as x = 3 + y, is invalid

rules.name: Substitute into remaining equations
rules.output_form: reduced system with one fewer variable in a target equation
preconditions: The isolated expression is equivalent to the original equation
rules.operation: Replace the isolated variable in the remaining equations by its equivalent expression.
examples: Substituting x = 3 - y into x - y = 1 gives 3 - y - y = 1
counterexamples: Substituting into only part of an equation is invalid

rules.name: Back-substitution
rules.input_form: solved value for one variable and an earlier relation
preconditions: The earlier relation remains valid for the current system
rules.operation: Recover remaining variable values after solving for one variable.
examples: After finding y = 1, substitute into x + y = 3 to get x = 2
counterexamples: Reporting a partial assignment as a complete solution is invalid

rules.name: Align variables for elimination
rules.input_form: two equations with a target elimination variable
rules.output_form: scaled or arranged equations with opposite coefficients
preconditions: The target variable appears in both equations with controllable coefficients
rules.operation: Prepare a pair of equations so a chosen variable will cancel under addition or subtraction.
examples: x + y = 3 and x - y = 1 already align for eliminating y by addition
counterexamples: Eliminating mismatched variables without coefficient control is invalid

rules.name: Eliminate a variable by addition or subtraction
rules.output_form: reduced equation with one fewer variable
preconditions: A chosen variable has opposite or matching coefficients suitable for cancellation
rules.operation: Combine equations so one variable cancels.
examples: Adding x + y = 3 and x - y = 1 gives 2x = 4
counterexamples: Combining equations and failing to cancel correctly is invalid

rules.name: Solve reduced equation and recover remaining variables
rules.input_form: single-variable reduced equation and original system relation
preconditions: The reduced equation was derived equivalently from the original system
rules.operation: Solve the reduced equation, then back-substitute into an original or equivalent relation.
examples: 2x = 4 gives x = 2, then x + y = 3 gives y = 1
counterexamples: Recovering remaining variables from a transformed equation that lost needed information can be invalid

rules.name: Coefficient matrix representation
preconditions: The system is linear
rules.operation: Represent a linear system in matrix-vector form.
examples: The system 2x + y = 5 and x - y = 1 corresponds to A = [[2,1],[1,-1]]
counterexamples: Non-linear systems do not fit this linear matrix form directly

rules.name: Augmented matrix representation
rules.input_form: coefficient matrix A and constant vector b
preconditions: The ordering of variables is fixed consistently
rules.operation: Attach the constant column to the coefficient matrix for row-operation workflows.
examples: [A|b] stores the system in row-operation form
counterexamples: Mixing coefficient and constant columns incorrectly changes the system

rules.name: Unique solution case
preconditions: Reduction yields one value for each variable and no free variables
rules.operation: Classify the system as having a unique solution.
examples: x + y = 3 and x - y = 1 has unique solution (2,1)
counterexamples: Free variables indicate the solution is not unique

rules.name: Inconsistent system case
preconditions: Reduction yields a contradiction such as 0 = 5
rules.operation: Classify the system as inconsistent.
examples: x + y = 1 and x + y = 3 are inconsistent together
counterexamples: Treating a contradiction row as harmless is invalid

rules.name: Infinitely many solutions case
rules.input_form: reduced system with dependent equations and free variables
preconditions: At least one free variable remains and no contradiction is present
rules.operation: Classify the system as having infinitely many solutions.
examples: x + y = 2 and 2x + 2y = 4 have infinitely many solutions
counterexamples: Claiming uniqueness when a free parameter remains is invalid

rules.name: Invalid equation-by-equation solution merge
rules.input_form: independent equation solutions merged without simultaneous check
rules.operation: Mark independent solution merging without simultaneous validation as invalid.
counterexamples: Values valid for one equation but not the other are not system solutions

rules.name: Invalid elimination arithmetic
rules.input_form: equations combined without coefficient alignment or correct arithmetic
rules.operation: Mark naive elimination without compatible coefficients or correct arithmetic as invalid.
counterexamples: x + 2y = 5 and x + y = 3 do not cancel y by naive subtraction unless arithmetic is done correctly

rules.name: Gaussian elimination step
rules.input_form: matrix row set or equation system with pivot row
rules.output_form: equivalent system with zeros introduced below a pivot
preconditions: A pivot entry has been chosen
The applied row operation is valid
rules.operation: Use a valid row operation to eliminate entries below a pivot and move the system toward echelon form.
examples: Subtracting 2 times the first row from the second can eliminate a leading coefficient below the pivot
counterexamples: Changing only part of a row is invalid

rules.name: Read solution from row-echelon form
preconditions: The system has been reduced to echelon form
rules.operation: Solve pivot variables from the bottom upward and identify any free variables.
examples: If the last row gives y = 1 and the row above gives x + y = 3, then x = 2
counterexamples: Reading a free variable as uniquely determined is invalid

rules.name: Nonzero determinant implies unique solution
preconditions: A is square
det(A) != 0
rules.operation: Use a nonzero determinant to conclude invertibility and uniqueness.
examples: A 2x2 system with determinant 5 has exactly one solution
counterexamples: Determinant reasoning in this form does not apply directly to nonsquare systems

rules.name: Zero determinant blocks inverse-based uniqueness
preconditions: A is square
det(A) = 0
rules.operation: Use determinant zero to rule out inverse-based unique solving while leaving consistency to further analysis.
examples: Two proportional equations give determinant 0 and no inverse-based unique solution
counterexamples: Determinant 0 does not by itself decide between inconsistency and infinitely many solutions

rules.name: Least-squares normal equations
rules.input_form: overdetermined system Ax approximately equals b
preconditions: The least-squares formulation is active
Matrix products are well-defined
rules.operation: Translate an overdetermined least-squares problem into its normal equations.
examples: A line-fit problem reduces to normal equations for the coefficient vector
counterexamples: Treating an inconsistent overdetermined system as exactly solvable without approximation is invalid

rules.name: Inverse matrix solution rule
preconditions: A is invertible
rules.operation: Solve a square system by left-multiplying with the inverse matrix.
examples: For invertible A, left-multiplying Ax = b by A^(-1) isolates x
counterexamples: Using A^(-1)b when A is singular is invalid

rules.name: Rank-based consistency check
rules.input_form: coefficient matrix A and augmented matrix [A|b]
preconditions: The ranks are computed correctly
rules.operation: Use rank equality or inequality between A and [A|b] to classify consistency and uniqueness structure.
examples: Equal coefficient and augmented ranks certify consistency
counterexamples: rank(A) < rank([A|b]) signals inconsistency, not a solution family

rules.name: Canonical form normalization expansion
preconditions: Auto-expansion rule requires explicit domain assumptions and validation metadata
rules.operation: Rewrite expressions into a canonical form that preserves the active equivalence relation.
examples: x + y and y + x map to a shared canonical additive form in commutative settings
counterexamples: Applying canonicalization rules outside their preconditions is invalid
common_errors: Using auto-generated rules without confirming domain-specific assumptions

rules.name: Divisibility transitivity
rules.input_form: a divides b and b divides c
preconditions: All divisibility relations are interpreted over integers
rules.operation: Compose divisibility through an intermediate multiple.
examples: 2 divides 6 and 6 divides 24, so 2 divides 24
counterexamples: Replacing one divisibility premise by a nondivisibility statement invalidates the conclusion

rules.name: Euclidean division form
rules.output_form: a = bq + r with 0 <= r < b
rules.operation: Express integer division by quotient and constrained remainder.
counterexamples: 17 = 5*2 + 7 is invalid Euclidean division because the remainder is not less than 5

rules.name: gcd invariance under remainder reduction
rules.operation: Reduce gcd computation by one Euclidean remainder step.
counterexamples: Replacing a mod b with an unrelated remainder breaks the rule

rules.name: Euclidean algorithm termination rule
preconditions: Remainder reduction is applied correctly at each step
rules.operation: Continue remainder reduction until the remainder is zero; return the last nonzero remainder as the gcd.
counterexamples: Stopping before the zero remainder step can miss the gcd

rules.name: Bezout identity
rules.operation: Represent the gcd as an integer linear combination of the two inputs.
counterexamples: Claiming ax + by = 1 for non-coprime a and b is invalid

rules.name: Coprime criterion via gcd
rules.operation: Classify two integers as coprime exactly when their gcd is 1.
examples: 8 and 15 are coprime
counterexamples: 8 and 12 are not coprime because gcd(8,12) = 4

rules.name: Modular inverse existence criterion
rules.operation: Use coprimality to determine whether a multiplicative inverse exists modulo n.
examples: 3 has an inverse modulo 7 because gcd(3,7)=1
counterexamples: 6 has no inverse modulo 9 because gcd(6,9)=3

rules.name: Fundamental theorem of arithmetic
rules.output_form: prime factorization unique up to order
rules.operation: Factor a positive integer into primes uniquely up to permutation of factors.
counterexamples: Writing two different prime factorizations for the same positive integer is invalid up to ordering

rules.name: Free energy seed

rules.name: Electromagnetic wave seed
preconditions: The standard homogeneous source-free regime is active
rules.operation: Derive electromagnetic wave propagation from Maxwell structure.

rules.name: Gibbs measure seed
preconditions: A canonical statistical-mechanics setting is fixed
rules.operation: Assign Gibbs weights through exponential energy penalties normalized by the partition function.
examples: Higher-energy states are suppressed relative to lower-energy states according to the temperature scale
counterexamples: Assigning arbitrary unnormalized weights without ensemble structure is invalid

rules.name: Spacetime interval seed
rules.input_form: spacetime coordinates under an active metric convention
preconditions: A relativistic metric convention is fixed
rules.operation: Use metric structure to define invariant spacetime interval data.
examples: Coordinate changes may alter components while preserving interval-type invariant structure
counterexamples: Treating time and space as Euclidean coordinates under all relativistic transformations is invalid

rules.name: Reaction-diffusion seed
preconditions: Reaction and diffusion mechanisms are fixed on a spatial domain
rules.operation: Model coupled local reaction and spatial diffusion dynamics.
examples: Pattern formation can arise from interplay between local reactions and spatial diffusion
counterexamples: Ignoring spatial coupling while claiming reaction-diffusion dynamics is invalid

rules.name: Chemical kinetics mass-action seed
preconditions: A reaction network and rate constants are fixed
rules.operation: Build kinetic equations from stoichiometric reaction data under mass action.
examples: Nonlinear ODE systems in chemistry arise directly from reaction-network stoichiometry under mass action
counterexamples: Assigning arbitrary reaction exponents with no kinetic model justification is invalid

rules.name: Competitive equilibrium seed
rules.input_form: prices, allocations, and agent optimization data
preconditions: A standard competitive-market model is fixed
rules.operation: Recognize competitive equilibrium by joint individual optimality and market clearing.
examples: Equilibrium requires both individual optimality and aggregate consistency
counterexamples: Optimizing one agent in isolation does not determine market equilibrium

rules.name: Black-Scholes seed
rules.input_form: frictionless diffusion-based asset model and derivative claim
preconditions: The standard no-arbitrage diffusion assumptions hold
rules.operation: Model derivative valuation through the Black-Scholes-type pricing equation.
examples: No-arbitrage and diffusion assumptions lead to PDE-based option pricing structure
counterexamples: Applying Black-Scholes outside its modeling assumptions without adjustment is invalid

rules.name: Network diffusion seed
rules.input_form: graph-based population with interaction or threshold dynamics
preconditions: A graph or interaction network and update rule are fixed
rules.operation: Model spread or adoption through network-coupled state evolution.
examples: Adoption patterns can depend on local neighborhood state rather than on isolated individual parameters alone
counterexamples: Treating population interactions as completely structure-free loses the network model

rules.name: Signal detection seed
rules.input_form: latent signal-noise model with response threshold or psychometric data
preconditions: A probabilistic response model and discrimination setting are fixed
rules.operation: Model decision behavior through signal-noise separation or psychometric transition structure.
examples: Response accuracy can vary systematically with signal strength rather than as an unstructured yes-no outcome
counterexamples: Ignoring latent uncertainty while claiming a signal-detection model is invalid

rules.name: Entropy production seed
rules.input_form: irreversible process model with entropy accounting
preconditions: A standard irreversible-process interpretation and entropy balance are fixed
rules.operation: Impose nonnegative entropy production in the standard nonequilibrium setting.
examples: Dissipation distinguishes irreversible evolution from ideal reversible balance laws
counterexamples: Assigning negative total entropy production in a closed irreversible model is invalid in the standard setting

rules.name: Poynting flux seed
rules.input_form: electromagnetic field configuration with energy-balance interpretation
preconditions: A Maxwell-type field model with energy accounting is fixed
rules.operation: Encode electromagnetic energy transport through Poynting-flux balance.
examples: Wave propagation carries energy through space rather than only oscillating local field values
counterexamples: Treating electromagnetic energy as present with no transport structure is invalid in the standard flux setting

rules.name: FLRW symmetry seed
rules.input_form: homogeneous and isotropic cosmological spacetime model
preconditions: Homogeneity, isotropy, and an FLRW-type metric ansatz are fixed
rules.operation: Reduce cosmological relativistic structure to scale-factor dynamics under FLRW symmetry.
examples: Large-scale symmetry assumptions compress relativistic geometry into a small number of dynamical cosmological variables
counterexamples: Arbitrary anisotropic or inhomogeneous universes are not automatically FLRW models

rules.name: Friedmann expansion seed
rules.input_form: cosmological scale factor with curvature and energy-density data
preconditions: An FLRW-type cosmological model and matter-energy content are fixed
rules.operation: Relate cosmic expansion to curvature and matter-energy content through a Friedmann-type equation.
examples: Cosmological dynamics are encoded through scale-factor evolution rather than by static spatial geometry alone
counterexamples: Assuming cosmic expansion is independent of matter-energy content is invalid in the standard Friedmann setting

rules.name: Virial balance seed
rules.input_form: gravitationally bound astrophysical system under an averaging regime
preconditions: A bound astrophysical system and averaging assumptions are fixed
rules.operation: Constrain bulk astrophysical behavior through averaged kinetic-potential balance.
examples: Cluster or stellar-system scale estimates can be constrained through bulk balance instead of exact trajectory tracking for every constituent
counterexamples: Arbitrary nonequilibrium transients do not automatically satisfy virial balance identities without the required averaging regime

rules.name: SIR compartment seed
rules.input_form: population state partitioned into susceptible, infectious, and removed classes
preconditions: A compartment model and transmission/removal conventions are fixed
rules.operation: Model epidemiological evolution through coupled SIR state transfers.
examples: Outbreak growth and decline can be modeled by state transfers between population compartments rather than by one scalar trend alone
counterexamples: Ignoring interaction-driven transmission while claiming an SIR-style model is invalid

rules.name: Replicator dynamics seed
rules.input_form: population of strategies with payoff-dependent updates
preconditions: Strategy shares and payoff functions are fixed
rules.operation: Evolve population shares by payoff advantage relative to the population average.
examples: Strategies with above-average payoff increase share while below-average strategies decline in a competitive population model
counterexamples: Changing shares with no payoff-relative update structure is not automatically replicator dynamics

rules.name: Stochastic volatility seed
rules.input_form: asset-price model with evolving latent volatility state
preconditions: A diffusion-based asset model and stochastic volatility state are fixed
rules.operation: Couple asset-price evolution to a separate stochastic volatility process.
examples: Option-pricing structure can depend on both price uncertainty and volatility dynamics rather than on constant variance alone
counterexamples: Treating every diffusion-pricing model as constant-volatility Black-Scholes is invalid once volatility becomes state-dependent

rules.name: Partition function thermodynamic seed
rules.input_form: equilibrium ensemble with microscopic state-sum structure
preconditions: A standard equilibrium ensemble and temperature scale are fixed
rules.operation: Recover macroscopic thermodynamic quantities from partition-function structure.
examples: Free energy, entropy, and response quantities can be recovered from one partition-function object rather than by separate unrelated formulas
counterexamples: Arbitrary state weights without normalization and temperature structure are not automatically partition-function models

rules.name: Fluctuation response seed
rules.input_form: equilibrium observable fluctuations with weak perturbation data
preconditions: An equilibrium ensemble and weak-response regime are fixed
rules.operation: Relate equilibrium fluctuations to linear response in the standard statistical-mechanics regime.
examples: Observable variance can predict weak-response behavior near equilibrium instead of requiring a fully separate model
counterexamples: Strong nonequilibrium response does not automatically satisfy equilibrium fluctuation-response relations

rules.name: Hydrostatic balance seed
rules.input_form: large-scale atmospheric or oceanic vertical momentum structure
preconditions: A large-scale geophysical flow regime and gravity field are fixed
rules.operation: Reduce vertical momentum structure to hydrostatic pressure-gravity balance when the standard regime applies.
examples: Large-scale atmospheric and oceanic models often reduce vertical momentum structure to pressure-gravity balance
counterexamples: Rapidly accelerating vertical flows are not automatically hydrostatic

rules.name: Geostrophic balance seed
rules.input_form: rotating large-scale flow with horizontal pressure-gradient data
preconditions: A rotating-frame geophysical model and large-scale regime are fixed
rules.operation: Balance Coriolis and horizontal pressure-gradient forces in the standard geostrophic regime.
examples: Synoptic-scale atmospheric motion is often approximated through pressure-Coriolis balance rather than full acceleration terms
counterexamples: Small-scale or highly ageostrophic flows are not automatically geostrophic

rules.name: Reaction network conservation seed
preconditions: A reaction network and species-balance interpretation are fixed
rules.operation: Constrain chemical trajectories by stoichiometric conservation relations.
examples: Total atom counts or conserved moieties can constrain system trajectories before any numerical solve is attempted
counterexamples: Assuming every concentration can vary independently despite stoichiometric constraints is invalid

rules.name: Chemical equilibrium law seed
rules.input_form: reaction system with forward and reverse equilibrium structure
preconditions: A thermodynamic-kinetic equilibrium setting is fixed

counterexamples: Applying equilibrium laws unchanged to strongly driven nonequilibrium reactors is invalid

rules.name: Threshold cascade seed

rules.output_form: cascade condition and adoption spread pattern
preconditions: A graph, threshold rule, and seeded state are fixed
rules.operation: Trigger adoption cascades when local network thresholds are exceeded.

counterexamples: Treating every diffusion process as threshold-free independent contagion is invalid

rules.name: Centrality influence seed
rules.input_form: interaction network with candidate influence ranking
preconditions: A graph-mediated interaction model and centrality notion are fixed
rules.operation: Rank influence by structural centrality in the network.
examples: Intervention on a structurally central node may alter diffusion far more than intervention on a peripheral node
counterexamples: Assuming all nodes contribute equally regardless of graph position is invalid

rules.name: Psychometric curve seed
rules.input_form: stimulus intensity and response probability data
preconditions: A discrimination task and stimulus-response setting are fixed
rules.operation: Model response probability as a smooth psychometric transition across stimulus intensity.
examples: Discrimination performance is often modeled by graded threshold behavior rather than by one abrupt binary switch only
counterexamples: A raw accuracy percentage with no stimulus-response structure is not automatically a psychometric curve

rules.name: Drift diffusion decision seed
rules.input_form: sequential evidence stream with noise and decision boundaries
preconditions: An evidence-accumulation setting and decision thresholds are fixed
rules.operation: Model sequential choice through noisy evidence accumulation with absorbing decision boundaries.

counterexamples: Arbitrary delayed responses do not automatically arise from drift-diffusion evidence accumulation

rules.name: Seed Set Primitive Normalization

rules.operation: Create a basis-level overlay record before any constant, workflow, or prediction claim is promoted, while preserving source-family differences in how the basis is framed.
properties: The basis record stays overlay-scoped and is not merged into the base mathematics corpus.
The overlay preserves disagreements between source families instead of flattening them into a false consensus.
Downstream claims must point back to the normalized primitive record.

counterexamples: Treating the declared basis as already-validated foundational mathematics without provenance tracking.

common_errors: Promoting derived constants before the basis record is normalized.
Forgetting that branch links describe supporting math routes rather than endorsement of the FSOT claim itself.

dependency_links.note: Object normalization is required before overlay primitives can be tracked.

common_errors: Confusing a symbolic placeholder with a justified zero-parameter quantity.

rules.name: Falsifiability Class Split
rules.input_form: A candidate overlay prediction with provenance and dependency-tier metadata.

Category B claims represent formula-level failures that may not invalidate the core engine.

counterexamples: Treating all prediction failures as equally damaging without source-backed classification.

dependency_links.note: Prediction class assignment depends on the underlying dependency tier audit.

rules.name: Spindle Speed (RPM)
rules.input_form: cutting speed V_c, tool/workpiece diameter D
rules.output_form: N = (1000 * V_c) / (pi * D) in metric, or N = (12 * V_c) / (pi * D) in imperial
preconditions: V_c > 0
rules.operation: Calculate the required spindle speed in RPM from the recommended surface cutting speed.
counterexamples: Using the imperial formula for metric inputs results in vastly incorrect RPM
common_errors: Confusing tool diameter (milling) with workpiece diameter (turning)

rules.name: Feed Rate (Table Feed)
rules.input_form: feed per tooth f_z, number of flutes/teeth z, spindle speed N
preconditions: f_z > 0
rules.operation: Calculate the linear feed rate of the machine table.
examples: f_z = 0.1 mm/tooth, z = 4, N = 3000 RPM -> V_f = 1200 mm/min
counterexamples: Assuming feed rate is independent of spindle speed
common_errors: Forgetting to multiply by the number of effective flutes z

rules.name: Material Removal Rate (Milling)
rules.input_form: axial depth of cut a_p, radial depth of cut a_e, feed rate V_f
preconditions: a_p > 0
a_e > 0
V_f > 0
rules.operation: Calculate the volume of material removed per unit time.
examples: a_p = 5 mm, a_e = 2 mm, V_f = 1000 mm/min -> MRR = 10,000 mm^3/min
counterexamples: MRR falls to zero if no radial engagement exists
common_errors: Using cutting speed V_c instead of feed rate V_f

rules.name: Surface Roughness (Turning)
rules.input_form: feed per revolution f, tool nose radius r_epsilon
preconditions: r_epsilon > 0
rules.operation: Estimate theoretical surface roughness based on tool geometry and feed.
examples: f = 0.2 mm/rev, r_eps = 0.8 mm -> R_max â‰ˆ 6.25 Âµm
counterexamples: Vibration will cause actual Ra to exceed theoretical Ra
common_errors: Using feed per minute instead of feed per revolution

rules.name: Taylor Tool Life Equation
rules.input_form: cutting speed V_c, tool life T, constants C and n
rules.operation: Model the relationship between cutting speed and tool life.
examples: n=0.25, C=300, V_c=150 m/min -> T = 16 minutes
counterexamples: Equation breaks arbitrarily at extremely low cutting speeds
common_errors: Assuming constants are material-independent

rules.name: Average Chip Thickness
rules.input_form: feed per tooth f_z, radial depth a_e, tool diameter D
rules.operation: Calculate the average chip thickness to optimize feed for chip thinning.
counterexamples: If slotting (a_e = D), approximation is invalid; use h_m = f_z
common_errors: Ignoring chip thinning at low radial depths

rules.name: Cutting Power Required
rules.input_form: material removal rate MRR, specific cutting force k_c, efficiency eta
preconditions: eta > 0
eta <= 1
rules.operation: Determine the spindle motor power required.
examples: MRR = 100 cm^3/min, k_c = 2000 N/mm^2, eta=0.8 -> P â‰ˆ 4.16 kW
counterexamples: Dull tools significantly increase required k_c
common_errors: Ignoring drivetrain efficiency losses

rules.name: Tapping Feed Rate
rules.input_form: spindle speed N, thread pitch p
rules.operation: Calculate the exact Z-axis feed rate required for rigid tapping.
examples: M8x1.25 tap, N = 500 RPM -> V_f = 625 mm/min
counterexamples: Rigid tapping requires absolute synchronization versus floating holders
common_errors: Multiplying by threads per inch (TPI) instead of pitch

rules.name: Bending Deflection of End Mill
rules.input_form: cutting force F_c, tool length L, Youngs modulus E, moment of inertia I
preconditions: Tool modeled as cantilever beam
rules.operation: Calculate tool deflection under lateral cutting force.
examples: Doubling tool length increases deflection by 8x
counterexamples: Tapered tools violate uniform beam assumptions
common_errors: Treating HSS and Carbide as having equal rigidity

rules.name: FSOT Intrinsic Surface Roughness (Turning)
rules.input_form: feed f, tool radius r_eps, depth a_p, speed v_c, norm v_cnorm
preconditions: r_eps > 0
rules.operation: Predict true surface roughness using zero-free-parameter FSOT physical compensation.
examples: f=0.07, ap=0.25, vc=350 -> FSOT predicts 0.315 um, matching physical reality better than standard.
counterexamples: Standard math excludes ap and vc completely, missing thermodynamic and deflection realities.
common_errors: Using arbitrary ML weights instead of FSOT derived dimensionless constants.

rules.name: FSOT Thermodynamic Tool Life Decay
rules.input_form: speed V_c, constants C and n, reference speed V_ref, golden ratio phi
preconditions: V_c > 0
phi > 0
rules.operation: Predict real tool life bounding empirical Taylor coefficients with FSOT golden ratio entropy.
examples: V_c = 150, standard predicts 16 mins. FSOT predicts 14.2 mins due to harmonic resonance fatigue.
counterexamples: Taylor's equation implies infinite life at zero speed, missing oxidation and ambient entropy scales.
common_errors: Ignoring exponential thermal degradation beyond the Taylor baseline.

rules.name: FSOT Dynamic Deflection Resonance
rules.input_form: force F_c, length L, diameter D, modulus E, inertia I
rules.operation: Account for non-linear structural resonance using FSOT dimensional bounds.
examples: L=50, D=10. Standard delta=0.02mm. FSOT delta=0.021mm (capturing structural resonance).
counterexamples: Standard linear beam deflection completely ignores harmonic chatter frequencies induced by the L/D ratio.
common_errors: Treating the spindle/collet connection as infinitely rigid.

rules.name: FSOT True Cutting Power Draw
rules.input_form: removal rate MRR, specific force k_c, efficiency eta, MRR_norm
preconditions: MRR > 0
eta > 0
rules.operation: Predict the true electrical power load using FSOT spatial energy translation limits.
examples: MRR=100. Standard predicts 4.16 kW. FSOT predicts 4.32 kW due to load inefficiency flow.
counterexamples: Theoretical power scales perfectly linearly; real spindles experience exponentially worse torque loss at peak MRR.
common_errors: Assuming constant efficiency independent of the material load.
